newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin takes office on Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin takes office on Tuesday.

text.p: Lionel Jospin takes office as prime minister on Tuesday after a stunning left-wing victory in France's elections that analysts say could delay or weaken European Monetary Union (EMU).

Jospin will formally replace defeated centre-right premier Alain Juppe at 11 a.m. (0900 GMT) and will appoint his cabinet in the next 48 hours, aides to the 59-year-old former education minister said.

He was appointed on Monday by centre-right President Jacques Chirac who unwittingly precipitated the changing of France's political guard when he called a snap general election intended to consolidate his own hold on power.

But Chirac completely misjudged the mood of the public, angry at him for failing to carry out 1995 campaign promises to curb inflation and slash taxes and for the centre-right government's imposition of austerity policies to qualify France for EMU.
French voters inflicted a crushing defeat on the president's supporters on Sunday.

A humiliated and politically diminished Chirac will now have to rule in uneasy "cohabitation" with a left-wing cabinet that is sceptical of the EMU and opposed to its fiscal strictures, which critics see as deflationary at a time of high unemployment.

Analysts said the Socialist victory put in doubt France's ability to adhere to the budgetary rigour of a single European currency and the future of the European Union's pivotal Franco-German political axis.

Jospin served notice he would not consider implementing further austerity measures ahead of the introduction of the euro currency, planned for 1999. He has argued for a more flexible interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty's criteria for joining monetary union.
Jospin's Socialists lack an outright majority in parliament, leaving it dependent on the backing of other left-wingers like the Communists and ecologists who are more hostile to European integration.
Negotiations went on through Monday with the Communists who say they want to join a Jospin government but are trying to win policy commitments before they line up behind him.

The demands of the Communists, who won 38 of the Assembly's 577 seats to 274 for the non-Communist left, include relaxation of national budget criteria set for joining EMU, an idea which would inevitably soften the new European Union currency.
The 1992 Maastricht Treaty set a course for deeper European political and monetary union, including tough terms for a country's qualification for the euro.

Socialist party spokesman Francois Hollande said Jospin wanted all left-wing parties to join his government and would reopen talks on a so-called "stability pact" approved by EU leaders last year to limit their deficits once the euro takes effect.
"We want to have assurances the stability pact does not signify new austerity in France," Hollande told Reuters Financial Television.

The Socialist agenda to ease austerity policies seen as having aggravated French unemployment could trigger a clash with Germany, which insisted on the pact punishing countries whose deficit exceeds three percent of gross domestic product.
That is Germany's price for abandoning its cherished and stable deutschemark for the euro.

Other Communist demands included wage rises to trigger a consumer-led economic recovery and cutting the working week from 39 hours to 35 hours in order to slash France's record 12.8 percent unemployment rate.
Hollande said on Monday there could be no immediate broad action on salaries or taxes though some symbolic measures would be taken by July.
He said it would not be realistic to set specific wage scales before a cabinet was formed.
French financial markets recouped early losses after opening down on news of the left's victory in the vote for the National Assembly.
Speculation was rife as to what jobs would go to whom but the Communists were not expected to get any of the key ministries such as foreign affairs, finance, defence or the interior.

One possible job for the Communists was the Sports Ministry with the name of Patrick Braouezec most often mentioned. He is mayor of the working class Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, where the next football World Cup is to be held.
NATO leaders are also due to meet in July in Madrid.

"It is planned that Lionel Jospin will go to all these meetings," the source said. "It is quite normal that he should be with the president, all the more because he has to get to know the representatives from other countries."
Jospin said during the campaign ahead of a Socialist-led parliamentary election victory on Sunday that France would speak with one voice on the international scene.

But the Socialists are nonetheless at odds with Chirac over France's approval of an EU "stability pact" to limit budget deficits after the launch of a single currency, and have criticised the gradual reintegration of France into NATO.
